summary: Unity is a commercial real-time three-dimensional engine and editor. Its own files are not an exchange format: scenes, prefabs and asset bundles are read only by Unity, and an asset bundle is tied to the build target and editor version that wrote it. The base editor covers drawing, scenes, transforms, physics through the built-in engine, audio, level of detail, instancing, text and C# scripting; almost everything a shared world needs on top of that arrives as a separate installable package, so a claim that Unity supports something is usually a claim about a package rather than about the engine. The one part of Unity that is genuinely built for portability is the humanoid rig: a fixed list of named bones and a muscle space that lets an animation authored on one body play on a different body. A standards reader should watch four traps: Unity's Avatar asset is a retargeting map and not an avatar body format; a material is a reference to a shader, so appearance does not survive a move even between Unity's own drawing pipelines, let alone to another renderer; the coordinate system is left-handed while the neutral formats are right-handed; and the two neutral formats this map cares about most, the glTF transfer format and the OpenUSD scene description format, are not read by the base editor at all, one needing an official package and the other only an experimental one.

coverage.note: The engine draws scenes to pixels itself, but the only pipeline inside the base editor is the Built-In Render Pipeline, which Unity has marked deprecated; the modern pass structure and render graph live in the Scriptable Render Pipeline packages.

coverage.note: Unity's additive scene loading (LoadSceneMode.Additive) loads another scene with its own GameObjects, MonoBehaviours and physics into the current world. Each loaded scene runs its own scripts within the shared update loop. But Unity defines no formal containment boundary — no event propagation protocol between host and contained scenes, no consumption rule, and no stated boundary for third-party experience isolation.

coverage.note: Unity's networking (Netcode for GameObjects, Netcode for Entities) replicates state within a single game session. Cross-world state coupling — where one Unity world mutates another's state with nobody in either — is not a built-in capability. Developers can build it with application code, but the engine defines no such mechanism.
